articles.title: A Bright, Sun-splashed Future for Renewable Energy
articles.source: American Association for the Advancement of Science (AAAS)
articles.cleaned_content:
The coal-fired furnaces, smelters and steam engines that powered the earliest days of the Industrial Revolution may be long gone, but their legacy has cast a long shadow. Although oil, natural gas, nuclear and renewable energy technologies have diversified the world’s energy budget since then, coal has long reigned as the single most dominant energy source at the global scale.

But in 2025, something remarkable happened: for the first time since the Industrial Revolution, renewable energy use surpassed coal burning as a source of electricity worldwide. Solar and wind power together account for most of that total, with hydropower and other renewables adding meaningful contributions. But it’s the explosive growth of solar, driven by key policy shifts and voracious global demand for affordable photovoltaic (PV) panels produced at scale, that has pushed renewables into the lead.

For their role in championing the global ascendancy of renewable energy, the Mani L. Bhaumik Breakthrough of the Year Award is being awarded to Charlie Gay, co-founder of the Greenstar Foundation; Hans-Josef Fell, president of Energy Watch Group; and Li Junfeng, standing director of the China Energy Research Society.

Recognizing the people behind such significant scientific developments is a central philosophy for donor Mani L. Bhaumik, Ph.D. — a physicist with myriad contributions to the development of high-powered lasers — as well as for AAAS and the Science family of journals.

“It’s impressive enough to invent a new technology, or to engineer a new way to harness that technology more effectively. But it’s another matter entirely to have a hand in seeing that technology achieve unparalleled global impact,” said Bhaumik. “I’m thrilled to see this year’s award bestowed on three pioneers who have advanced renewable energy on multiple fronts, over many decades.”

The Mani L. Bhaumik Breakthrough of the Year Award was established in 2022 with an $11.4 million pledge from Bhaumik — the largest in the organization’s history. The award supports a $250,000 annual cash prize for up to three scientists or researchers whose work best underpins the Science Breakthrough of the Year , the journal’s choice of the top research advance of the year. In 2025, Science named renewable energy surpassing coal as the latest Breakthrough.

“These three critical players have each had a broad impact over multiple decades, including roles in technology, policy, and market development,” said Robert Margolis, a former senior energy analyst at the National Renewable Energy Laboratory (NREL; now the National Laboratory of the Rockies), and a member of the committee that selected the winners, convened by the Science journals’ Editor-in-Chief Holden Thorp. “It’s taken on the order of 50 years to go from invention to a real market. Each winner has demonstrated a long-term commitment to helping the technology develop, but also to fostering advancements in manufacturing and policy.”

For the committee, this wide-angle view was paramount. Each agreed it was important to look beyond science and engineering alone, to the deliberate policy and market measures that have bolstered renewables over the past half-century-plus, after the United States began installing PV cells on satellites in the late 1950s. Well into the 1990s, these PV cells were still quite expensive to build — and there was little certainty at the time that a market for widespread public and private use would ever materialize.

“Much of the technology arose from crucial inventions in the U.S., with public investment from NASA, NREL, and others. But Germany pioneered much of the policy around market formation, and China has made breakthroughs in manufacturing and process improvements that have substantially helped to reduce costs,” said committee member Kelly Sims Gallagher, a professor of energy and environmental policy and dean of the Fletcher School at Tufts University. “We recognized that this milestone could not have been achieved by one country alone. It’s a global phenomenon — the product of many global actors — and the winners we selected reflect this well.”

Combined, this year’s winners have more than a century’s worth of experience fostering the advancement of renewable energy, in both government and private enterprise. Their impressive and diverse track record spans science, engineering, policy and economic development.

After starting his career in research in the 1970s, Gay helped to advance the design of solar panels, including by adapting low-cost screen printing techniques as well as manufacturing approaches borrowed from the automotive safety glass industry. Later, he served as director of NREL from 1994 to 1997, and then as director of the Department of Energy’s Solar Energy Technologies Office from 2016 to 2019. Through it all, he has embraced involvement in a wide variety of startup companies, advisory boards, industry councils and award juries.

A former schoolteacher, Fell first became involved in renewable energy at the grassroots level, then as a city council member in his hometown of Hammelburg, Germany, and later as a member of German Federal Parliament (Bundestag) representing the country’s Green Party from1998 to 2013. He is best known as a co-author of the 2000 German Renewable Energy Sources Act, which created the world’s first “feed-in tariff” to pay private citizens, companies and energy communities for solar and other renewable energy they put back into the power grid.

Widely known as the lead author of China’s Renewable Energy Law, Li began his career in the 1980s, working to bring affordable renewable technologies to rural areas. Later, he helped to launch training programs for renewable energy entrepreneurs, which fueled the development of several major Chinese companies. He has held a wide variety of leadership roles, including with the National Center for Climate Change Strategy and International Cooperation and the Chinese Renewable Energy Industries Association.

A brief history of the solar revolution

While they account for ever-more important slices of the global energy pie, wind power and hydropower are not new. The first windmills and watermills appeared centuries ago, to power a wide variety of agricultural and manufacturing tasks directly. Their modern derivatives — wind turbines and hydroelectric dams — now generate electricity that can be transported or stored for a wide variety of uses.

By comparison, solar energy is the new kid on the block. As Bhaumik Award winner Li Junfeng explains, the solar story began in Paris, France, in 1839. “The first important milestone is the scientific discovery of the photovoltaic effect by French scientist Edmond Becquerel, laying the physical foundation for solar power generation,” Li said. The next half century was relatively quiet, until 1905, when “Albert Einstein theoretically explained the photoelectric effect, clarifying the conversion mechanism from photons to electricity, for which he was awarded the Nobel Prize in 1921. Without these fundamental discoveries, solar cells would never have been invented,” Li added.

Another half century passed until 1954, when U.S.-based Bell Laboratories created the world’s first practical solar panel made of monocrystalline silicon. Four years later, in 1958, the Naval Research Laboratory installed solar panels on the Vanguard 1 satellite, demonstrating the technology’s capabilities in high-stakes aerospace applications. Then, in 1973, researchers at the University of Delaware quite literally brought the technology back down to Earth by building the world’s first solar-powered residential house. “This opened a new era for PV to expand from aerospace to terrestrial civilian applications,” Li explained.

Later in 1973, the first oil embargo sent oil prices skyrocketing, and by comparison, solar power’s future began to look very bright indeed. Bhaumik Award winner Charlie Gay remembers chatting that year with Eugene Ralph, co-founder of Spectrolab, who had drawn a chart to show how much costs had already come down because of the market to install PV cells on satellites.

“As it turns out, that trajectory he put on a small piece of graph paper has held for the last 50 years; for every cumulative doubling of the amount of solar, costs have come down somewhere in the ballpark of 28% to 30%,” Gay said. “And that predictability that comes with scale is really differentiating. It’s the ability to know that if you build more, you can get the cost down. The same has held true for everything from integrated circuits to broiler chickens. Predictable cost reduction gives investors confidence that market elasticity will kick in, then you get more customers.”

The lion’s share of work to develop solar technology happened in the U.S., driven by both public and private investment. Gay emerged as a leader during this time, recognized by colleagues for his work to bridge the gaps between scientific discoveries, engineering advances and industrial realities.

“The first solar cells were something of a niche product, and it could have been easy for them to fall into an R&D ‘valley of death’ at that point,” said committee member Joseph Berry, a senior research scientist at the National Laboratory of the Rockies. “We wanted to recognize somebody who was important in that early transition, who went from research into an industrial setting to enable improvements to the technology.”

Berry noted that he worked with Gay in the 2010s, when Gay served as director of the Department of Energy’s Solar Energy Technologies Office.

“Charlie's perspective is something I got to witness firsthand; it's not enough to have a nice result that's lab scale, you really have to do it in a way that matters,” Berry said. “You have to consider how it will ultimately be deployed, and that means engaging with industry and understanding their constraints.”

“Charlie really epitomizes the type of person who can wear multiple hats over a long career, with a commitment to helping technology through that innovation-to-manufacturing process,” Margolis agreed. “When you look at Charlie’s history, he was involved in practically every company that was important in the U.S. at one point or another.”

Against this backdrop of ever-improving solar cell technology and slow but steady industrial scale-up, another crisis soon presented the world with a watershed moment: the 1986 Chernobyl nuclear disaster. The explosion sent enough radioactive material into the air to raise alarms at the Forsmark nuclear power plant in Sweden, more than 1,000 kilometers away. Soon, these literal alarms gave way to figurative ones.

“At this time, many people in Germany — especially those in associations and groups working to save the world from air pollution — wanted to cancel nuclear power and protect the climate,” Bhaumik Award winner Hans-Josef Fell explained. “They soon found out that solar and wind power together with bioenergy, hydropower, geothermal, marine energy and energy storage technologies are the best options to advance those goals. These sources of renewable energy are abundant all over the world. We had no scarcity of supply, only a scarcity of technology.”

Fell described a groundswell of local-scale organizing and investment. He began in 1991 by installing a modest solar panel system on his own home, which quickly led to interest from his friends and others in the community. Before long, he was seeing interest grow nationwide — and beyond.

“In Germany and plenty of other regions — in California, for example — we saw this big grassroots movement from the bottom up to create practical, realistic renewable energy solutions,” Fell said. “When people asked for these technologies, companies could see they have a market, so they invested in production. When politicians saw this increasing demand from consumers and companies, they saw the need for a better policy framework.”

Building a foundation for 21st century investment

By the 1990s, costs to implement solar power were beginning to come down in a meaningful way, while demand was steadily increasing. The stage was nearly set for explosive growth. Yet, many countries and localities lacked the strong policy framework that Fell and others had identified as a pressing need. Enter the feed-in tariff, a mechanism designed to offset the costs of individual private investments in renewable electricity infrastructure, by offering guaranteed long-term purchase rates for power fed back into the grid.

“The world’s first feed-in tariffs for solar power were done in three towns and cities in Germany: my hometown of Hammelburg, as well as Freising and Aachen,” Fell explained. “As a member of the town council who helped to decide this matter, I first learned how to make such a law. I also learned how to create a community that can invest into solar power systems.”

Fell and his colleagues soon created the world’s first solar community in Hammelburg. “We asked people to invest with the hope that we can get back our financing in 20 years by selling our electricity,” he explained. “Normally, it would be hard to find people willing to invest on a 20-year timetable, but we found a lot of them. Some years later, many other communities and cooperatives followed our example.”

Fell’s motivation to make solar accessible to all of Germany led him to the Bundestag. There, he pursued what would become his most notable achievement: drafting the world’s first national feed-in tariff policy. Then, in partnership with his colleague Hermann Scheer, he helped to organize a Bundestag majority to pass the law despite strong political headwinds. The Renewable Energy Sources Act (Erneuerbare-Energien-Gesetz, or EEG) became law in 2000 and soon served as a template for many other countries.

Fell and Scheer advocated for the EEG across the world, actively engaging with global governments through informal discussions and official hearings. Fell also visited China several times as a board member of the German-Chinese Parliamentary Group, where he promoted the adoption of a nationwide equivalent to the EEG in China.

“The feed-in tariff was such a crucial development. It offered a stable, clear investment incentive for renewable energy in Germany,” Gallagher said. “In 2010, I was interviewing a lot of Chinese manufacturers. Many pointed to Germany, and also Spain by this point, as providing early important markets for Chinese imports. They weren’t initially producing for their own domestic market. Now China has implemented their own renewable energy law, and the domestic market has taken off. In the U.S., state-level incentives have taken off.”

“The German national law is a big part of what brought the Chinese into the space. If they could manufacture at scale, there would be a market,” Margolis agreed. “As more countries passed similar laws, it really increased demand. We started to see cost reductions at the system level, not just the module level, which really catalyzed scaling up the broader solar supply chain.”

Driven by burgeoning global demand and enabled by relentless innovation, China now leads the world in both the production and installation of new solar cells. At the heart of it all, Li has been a steady advocate for strategic policy interventions at home and impactful international collaborations abroad. Building on the example set by Germany, Li shepherded the creation and passage of the Renewable Energy Law of the People’s Republic of China, enacted in 2005.

“As the principal architect of China’s feed-in tariff, Li is considered the father of renewable energy in China,” Gallagher said. “He has such a comprehensive view, and gave a lot of consideration to which policies would be most effective initially, to spur industry to develop. He stands out as the person who most consistently thought out a coherent strategy.”

Renewable energy was once a radical idea in China. Historically dependent on coal, the country continues to build new coal-fired power plants, to hedge against potential shortfalls as the country continues to grow and develop. Yet for the past several years, China has repeatedly set and broken new records for renewable energy installation. This explosion of Chinese solar capacity has greatly helped to push renewable energy beyond coal power globally in 2025.

Li said that in the last 15 to 20 years, global solar cell manufacturers have substantially raised cell efficiency while cutting material and power consumption in manufacturing. These measures have lowered production costs, expanded market demand, and enabled full-scale mass production.

Although the basic silicon-based chemistry of solar cells hasn’t changed much since the first commercially available units came on the market, efficiency increases thanks to continual engineering refinements have made all the difference. As Li explains, much of that increase is very recent.

“The first Bell Labs solar cell achieved only about 6% efficiency; by 2010, it had reached roughly 16%, a gain of merely 10 percentage points over more than 50 years,” he said. “By 2025, solar cell efficiency has climbed to 28%, adding another 12 percentage points in 15 years.”

Silicon — specifically, a highly purified form known as monocrystalline silicon — forms the beating heart of solar cells, cut into hair-thin wafers that harvest sunlight and convert it to electricity. This material is first crystallized from polysilicon feedstock. While the cost of polysilicon has come down over the years, process improvements have also reduced the amount needed to build new cells. Here again, determined Chinese manufacturers have yielded notable improvements.

“In the 1970s, polysilicon consumption exceeded 100 grams per watt. It still remained above 15 grams in 2000, an 85% reduction over three decades,” Li said. “Since 2010, polysilicon consumption dropped to around 2 grams per watt by 2025 — another 85% reduction within only 15 years, or half the time.”

While celebrating China’s successes, Li also acknowledged that the continued refinement and adoption of solar power will be a worldwide undertaking.

“The global success of PV technology owes a debt to scientists, engineers, entrepreneurs and policymakers. Meanwhile, consumers worldwide have made indelible contributions by creating continuous market demand that nurtured the birth, growth and maturity of the renewable energy industry,” he said. “The achievements of renewable energy represent collective global endeavors, and its technological dividends should benefit every corner of the world.”

Only time will tell where the ceiling may be for solar power in the years ahead. Among other plausible future developments, hundreds of scientists worldwide are investigating the potential of perovskite compounds as alternatives to polysilicon. While they show promise to exceed the efficiencies of silicon panels, for now, perovskite’s key weakness is long-term stability and durability.

Either way, Li has some ambitious predictions for what’s to come in the next decade. By 2030, he anticipates that non-fossil power (all renewables combined with nuclear power) will overtake all fossil fuels in terms of total power generation. By 2035, he suspects that renewables alone will reach this benchmark, surpassing all fossil fuels to become the world’s primary energy sources.

For his part, Gay envisions solar energy as a lever that could one day enable homeowners to participate in a shared energy and information economy.

“The home itself could be a data center, part of a living solution to how we meet energy needs. Solar on the rooftop, a battery in the garage, and the ability to move information at light speed,” he said. “Centralized power generation will soon be the old-school way to provide electricity. It carried us through most of the industrial era, but today energy and information are scaling in parallel. Distributed servers, one in every home, can meet the needs of the home and also plug into the grid.”

Fell anticipates that the unstoppable momentum of solar energy will extend to other renewable technologies and storage systems, much as a rising tide will lift all boats. As demand for solar continues to reach new heights, consumers will soon yearn for improvements to other technologies to help fill the gaps.

“Wind energy will continue to be the most important addition to solar. Wind blows more at night and in wintertime, making it a natural addition to balance at times when solar is not productive,” Fell said. “And the current technology can create huge amounts of energy that seemed impossible only 10 years ago.”

Fell foresees a future with 100% renewable energy across all energy-use sectors, including electric power, transportation, industrial, residential and commercial consumption. In such a system, he estimates solar power will likely make up about 60% of the total, with wind covering about 30%. The last 10% will come from other sources, such as bioenergy, hydropower (including freestanding water turbines that do not block river flow), geothermal energy and marine wave energy.

“Whatever the road ahead may bring, these three renewable energy pioneers have done so much to set the world up for continued success,” said Science Editor-in-Chief Holden Thorp. “Our energy future looks very bright indeed.”

articles.title: Freezing fire: UT San Antonio scientists discover breakthrough for green energy
articles.cleaned_content:
Freezing fire: UT San Antonio scientists discover breakthrough for green energy

As the global push for cleaner energy intensifies, solid oxide fuel cells have emerged as a promising option. They turn hydrogen or other renewable fuels directly into electricity and heat without combustion, eliminating virtually all pollution and boosting efficiency to over 60%. But a major downside has kept them out of everyday commercial use: they require extremely high temperatures to operate.

A team of researchers at UT San Antonio and partnering institutions have found a way around that barrier. Instead of relying on perfectly ordered materials, they applied a thermal shock technique to create tiny clusters of disordered atoms that move oxygen ions much more easily at lower temperatures. The result could help make fuel cells cheaper, more durable and easier to use outside the lab.

“The golden rule has been that you need a perfect crystal lattice for fast ion movement,” said Chonglin Chen , PhD, a professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the College of Sciences. “What we have done here challenges that assumption.”

The team recently published their findings in Science Advances , with Shengli Pang , a Jiangsu University researcher and member of Chen’s team, serving as the lead author.

Conventional solid oxide fuel cells (SOFCs) operate “inadequately” at temperatures lower than 400 degrees Celsius, making them incredibly difficult to use in commercial settings, Chen explained.

Conventional SOFCs need extreme temperatures, often exceeding 700°C, to operate. These volcanic temperatures accelerate material breakdown, demand expensive heat-resistant components to contain the heat, and cause long startup delays.

To solve this problem, the team turned to molecular nanotechnology, using extreme temperature swings to create materials with helpful imperfections at the atomic level.  First, they baked a standard ceramic fuel cell material at a scorching 1,300°C. They then rapidly froze it through a technique called quenching — plunging it into liquid nitrogen at nearly –196°C. This violent temperature shock shatters the material’s rigid, glass-like structure into ultra-thin, microscopic clusters of atoms measuring just 0.63 nanometers thick — so small that thousands of them could stack across the width of a single human hair.

Chen said the idea came from steelmaking, where quenching is used to change the material’s structure. The team adapted that approach for ceramics and found that the resulting clusters conducted oxygen ions far better than expected.

When tested at 400°C, the material achieved record oxygen-ion conductivity, about 1,400 times higher than a conventional ceramic material.

The breakthrough challenges a longstanding assumption in materials science that the best conductors must have a perfectly ordered, rigid crystal structure, with the neat rows of atoms acting like well-defined lanes on a highway.

But when the team examined their new material with electron microscopes and X-ray analysis, they found that the atoms inside these tiny fragments were disordered and chaotic. Yet they were still performing well.

This is because in traditional materials, the atomic-scale paths eventually become blocked as atoms clump together under stress, creating bottlenecks that interrupt the energy flow. But inside the new, disordered nanoclusters were oxygen vacancies that stayed separate and active, while interacting to create a network that allowed ions to travel more freely.

“With these vacancy-isolated clusters, we created a chaotic, highly dynamic network where the oxygen vacancies remain independent,” Chen explained. “Instead of fighting the disorder, we are using it to create a kind of superhighway for the ions.”

What this means for clean energy

To demonstrate commercial viability, the team tested whether the material could improve real fuel cell performance. By blending a trace amount of the clusters — just 0.5% by weight — with a conventional cobalt-based fuel cell cathode, they tripled the fuel cell’s peak power output.

In addition to boosting power, the clusters also boost durability. Standard fuel cells degrade quickly, losing over 13% of their power every 100 hours of use under the intense stress of high temperatures. But fuel cells enhanced with the disordered nanoclusters became 3.4% more stable and efficient with continued use.

“It acts as an atomic shield, boosting power while actively stopping the degradation that normally kills these devices,” Chen said.

Chen believes that the method could be easy for manufacturers to adopt because it requires only a small amount of the new material rather than a complete redesign of existing systems. They are now working on ways to scale up production.

“This will bring us one step closer to practical, next-generation green energy,” Chen added.

articles.title: New fuel cell breakthrough could help power energy-hungry data centers
articles.cleaned_content:
New fuel cell breakthrough could help power energy-hungry data centers

A new ultra-durable fuel-cell catalyst could help turn hydrogen into a more practical power source for energy-hungry data centers and beyond.

The rapid expansion of data centers across the United States is putting growing pressure on the nation's electricity supply. These facilities require enormous amounts of power not only to operate their computing equipment, but also to keep it cool. The Electric Power Research Institute estimates that data centers could account for as much as 9% of annual U.S. electricity generation by 2030, compared with 4% of total electricity demand in 2023.

Researchers are now exploring ways to reduce some of that strain. A team led by Gang Wu, the Elvera and William R. Stuckenberg Professor in the McKelvey School of Engineering at Washington University in St. Louis, has developed an approach that could improve low-temperature fuel cells and potentially expand their use as an alternative source of electricity.

The research team also included scientists from Brookhaven National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Northeastern University and the University of Pittsburgh. Their findings were published Aug. 6, 2026, in Nature Nanotechnology .

"If a data center is able to supply its electricity itself by using a fuel cell, it would directly convert hydrogen and other fuels into the electricity, reducing the burden on the energy grid," Wu said.

Making Fuel Cells More Efficient and Durable

Fuel cells produce electricity by combining hydrogen and oxygen. The process also generates water and heat. Catalysts help accelerate this reaction while limiting energy losses and supporting stronger performance and longer operating life.

Designing the right catalyst remains a major challenge. Existing fuel cell catalysts still struggle to provide the combination of activity and durability needed to meet important performance goals.

Platinum is considered one of the most effective catalyst materials, but it is also a precious metal. Researchers therefore want to use as little platinum as possible without reducing the catalyst's effectiveness during energy conversion and storage.

One way to stretch a small amount of platinum further is to turn it into nanoparticles. Breaking bulk platinum into extremely small particles dramatically increases the amount of surface exposed for chemical reactions. This makes it possible to use very small quantities of the metal, typically less than one quarter of a milligram per square centimeter.

The problem is that platinum nanoparticles can change during fuel cell operation. They may dissolve, move to different locations, and grow larger, causing performance to gradually decline.

A Longstanding Platinum Catalyst Challenge

More recently, platinum intermetallic catalysts have emerged as a promising alternative to conventional platinum alloys because they can offer improved activity and stability.

Producing them, however, involves another difficult compromise. To keep the nanoparticles small, evenly distributed and efficient in their use of platinum, researchers generally anneal the materials at temperatures below 700°C. Those temperatures are often too low to fully trigger the transition from a disordered atomic arrangement to a highly ordered one, which is important for maximizing both the activity and durability of intermetallic catalysts.

Wu and his colleagues developed a new carbon structure designed to overcome this limitation. The material consists of porous, hollow carbon spheres containing orderly radial nanochannels, along with substantial pore space and surface area.

This structure allows large numbers of platinum cobalt intermetallic nanoparticles to remain densely packed yet evenly distributed. It also makes it possible to form the desired ordered intermetallic structure at much higher temperatures without causing the nanoparticles to clump together.

In this way, the researchers were able to address a difficult tradeoff between achieving a highly ordered atomic structure and maintaining an even distribution of very small catalyst particles.

"Our strategy is using this new carbon nanostructure to synthesize platinum cobalt intermetallic nanoparticles that can reduce precious metal content and enhance activity and stability," Wu said. "Traditionally, there would be a tradeoff between size and stability, but with the ordered carbon nanochannel host, platinum cobalt nanoparticles can be confined and remain stable at very small particle size even at high temperatures."

Tiny Carbon Channels Help Platinum Last Longer

Larger catalyst particles can improve stability, but that often comes at the expense of activity. Other approaches that prioritize activity may sacrifice long-term stability.

Wu's team sought to achieve both by creating a nanostructured carbon support with tiny channels arranged in a radial pattern. The researchers also carefully controlled the size and volume of the pores.

In testing, the material retained 85% of its performance after 150,000 severe voltage cycles. The researchers estimate that this could correspond to roughly 25,000 hours of operation. Its combination of larger pores, carefully organized pore sizes, and high surface area helped the catalyst overcome the usual tradeoff between activity and stability.

"Because of this special carbon nanostructured support, we could heat the platinum-cobalt catalyst to 1000°C, which is high enough to form a very ordered structure while still keeping the nanoparticles smaller than 5 nanometers and well spread out, even with industry-preferred high content of platinum in catalysts," Wu said.

Heating the catalyst to such a high temperature allowed its atoms to form the ordered structure needed for stronger performance. At the same time, the carbon support kept the platinum cobalt nanoparticles smaller than 5 nanometers and prevented them from becoming unevenly distributed.

A Potential Path Toward Better Fuel Cell Power

The architecture of the carbon support offers additional benefits beyond stabilizing the nanoparticles. Its open channels help materials involved in transporting ions spread more uniformly through the electrode. They also provide easier pathways for protons, oxygen, and water to move.

"The open channel structure also helps the ion-containing material, such as an ionomer, spread evenly and makes it easier for protons, oxygen and water to move through the electrode," Wu continued. "As a result, the platinum cobalt nanoparticles built into this support showed best-in-class performance and long-lasting durability. Eventually, through further development and collaboration with industry partners, we'll be able to solve the remaining catalyst problems and significantly advance fuel cell technologies for powering our future more efficiently and sustainably."

If further development proves successful, the technology could help improve fuel cells for applications ranging from transportation to electricity generation. For data centers in particular, fuel cells could offer a way to generate electricity directly from hydrogen or other fuels, potentially reducing some of the growing demand placed on the electric grid.

Wu has filed a patent on the technology through the WashU Office of Technology Management.

The research was funded by Washington University in St. Louis. Collaborating institutions included Brookhaven National Laboratory, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Northeastern University and the University of Pittsburgh.

articles.title: California's Plug-In Solar Breakthrough Marks Major Milestone for National Renewable Energy Movement
articles.cleaned_content:
Bright Saver celebrates SB 868 becoming law as California advances accessible solar energy and builds momentum for broader renewable energy adoption across the United States.

SAN FRANCISCO--(BUSINESS WIRE)-- Bright Saver today celebrated Governor Gavin Newsom's signing of SB 868, the Plug and Play Solar Act, marking a significant milestone for California and the growing national movement to make renewable energy more accessible to everyday Americans.

Authored by State Senator Scott Wiener, the legislation removes regulatory barriers to small, portable plug-in solar systems, commonly known as plug-in or balcony solar, while establishing safety requirements for their use. The law creates a new pathway for Californians to generate their own clean electricity and gain greater control over household energy costs.

For Bright Saver, a nonprofit working to accelerate the adoption of plug-in solar nationwide, California's action represents an important step toward a much larger goal: removing regulatory barriers to clean energy markets and enabling more Americans to participate in the clean energy transition.

“There's a reason people say, 'As California goes, so goes the nation.' This is a significant milestone, not just for plug-in solar, but for the broader movement to make clean energy accessible to everyone,” said Cora Stryker, Co-founder and Co-CEO of Bright Saver. “When we founded Bright Saver, we set out to remove the barriers that have kept everyday Americans from participating in the clean energy transition. Plug-in solar is one important step toward that vision. California's move sends a powerful signal to the rest of the country about what's possible when we make clean energy easier to adopt. This is a major victory for our movement, but we're just getting started.”

California joins a growing number of states advancing legislation to make plug-in solar more accessible. Its adoption is particularly significant given the state's market size, influence on national energy policy and longstanding role in accelerating clean energy innovation.

Unlike conventional rooftop solar installations, plug-in solar systems offer a smaller-scale entry point into clean energy ownership, allowing households to generate electricity without the cost and complexity of a traditional solar installation.

Bright Saver has been working to build national awareness, organize advocates and support state-level efforts to expand access to plug-in solar. With SB 868 now law, California adds new momentum to those efforts as advocates continue working toward broader adoption nationwide.

Bright Saver Participates in San Francisco Press Conference

Later today, Bright Saver will join Senator Wiener, Environmental Working Group (EWG), SPUR, and other clean energy champions at a press conference celebrating SB 868 and SB 222, legislation designed to streamline residential heat pump installations.

The event will take place at 11 a.m. at SPUR headquarters, 654 Mission Street, San Francisco.

Bright Saver will provide a plug-in solar panel for the demonstration, and Co-Founder and Co-CEO Cora Stryker will be available for media interviews on California's new plug-in solar law, the growing national movement and the broader effort to make renewable energy accessible to more Americans.

California's milestone is just the beginning. Bright Saver invites Americans across the country to join the growing movement to make clean energy more accessible and affordable. By contributing $29 a year, members can support advocacy, education, and efforts to expand plug-in solar adoption nationwide.

Join the movement at brightsaver.org .

Bright Saver is the first and only nonprofit in the United States dedicated to plug-in “balcony” solar. We believe that no American should have to choose between saving money and fighting climate change, and we have already helped pass laws in 11 states that make it easier for people to power their own homes with clean energy.

To learn more, get involved, or support Bright Saver's mission, visit brightsaver.org .
